en: Thus have I heard— The Middle Discourses 62: The Greater Discourse of Advice to Rāhula.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
The Venerable Rāhula also, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having looked around, addressed the Venerable Rāhula:
“Rāhula, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all form is ‘not mine,’ [not I, not my self].”
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
“Is it form alone, Blessed One? Is it form alone, Sugata?
“Form also, Rāhula, feeling also, Rāhula, perception also, Rāhula, volitional formations also, and consciousness also, Rāhula.”
Then the Venerable Rāhula thought, "Who else today will enter the village for alms after being exhorted by the Blessed One in his presence with an exhortation?
Thereupon, he turned back and sat down at the foot of a certain tree, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
The Venerable Sāriputta saw the Venerable Rāhula sitting at the foot of a certain tree, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.
Having seen him, he addressed the Venerable Rāhula:
“Rāhula, develop the meditation on mindfulness of breathing.”
“Rāhula, mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Rāhula emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable...
Rāhula said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it becomes of great fruit and great benefit?
“Rāhula, whatever internally, personally, is hard, solid, and clung-to, such as:”
Head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver,
midriff, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, gorge, feces, or whatever else there is internally,
belonging to oneself, that is hard, solid, and clung-to.
This, Rāhula, is called the internal earth element.
Now, both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply the earth element.
This should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
Having seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and detaches the mind from the earth element.
And what, Rāhula, is the water element?
The water element may be internal or it may be external.
And what, Rāhula, is the internal water element?
Whatever internally, within oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to (appropriated), namely:
bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, nasal mucus, synovial fluid, urine, or whatever else internally, within oneself, is water, watery, and clung-to.
This, Rāhula, is called the internal water element.
Now, both the internal water element and the external water element are simply the water element.
This should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
Having seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the water element and detaches the mind from the water element.
And what, Rāhula, is the fire element?
The fire element may be internal or it may be external.
And what, Rāhula, is the internal fire element?
Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is fire or fiery, and is grasped [as self], namely:
that by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is digested.
Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is fire or fiery, clung-to (upādinna)— this, Rāhula,
is called the internal fire element.
Now, both the internal fire element and the external fire element are simply the fire element.
"This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element and detaches the mind from the fire element.
And what, Rāhula, is the air element?
The air element may be internal or it may be external.
And what, Rāhula, is the internal air element?
Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is air or airy, and is clung-to, such as:

Upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, winds moving in the belly, winds moving in the bowels, winds following through the limbs and members, inhalation and exhalation, or whatever else internally and personally is wind,
windy-natured, and clung-to— this, Rāhula, is called the internal air element.
And that which is the internal air element and that which is the external air element are both simply the air element.
"This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element and detaches the mind from the air element.
And what, Rāhula, is the space element?
The space element may be internal or external.
And what, Rāhula, is the internal space element?
That which is internal, belonging to oneself, space, of the nature of space, and clung-to; that is to say:
The ear-cavities, the nostril-cavities, the mouth-opening; that by which one swallows what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted;
where what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted remains; that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted issues out from the lower part;
or whatever else there is internally, belonging to oneself, that is space, spatial, a void.
That which is internal, void, voidness, unobstructed, not touched by flesh and blood, and clung-to— this, Rāhula,
is called the internal space element. Now, both the internal space element and the external space element are simply the space element.
"This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the space element and detaches the mind from the space element.
Rāhula, cultivate the meditation that is like the earth.
For when you, Rāhula, cultivate the meditation that is like the earth, pleasant and unpleasant contacts that arise will not persist by taking possession of your mind.
Just as, Rāhula, they place clean things on the earth, they place unclean things on it;
they place excrement there, urine there, spittle there, and pus there.
They even discard blood, yet the earth is neither repelled, nor ashamed, nor disgusted by it.
In the same way, Rāhula, develop the meditation that is like the earth.
For as you develop this earth-like meditation, Rāhula, pleasant and unpleasant contacts that arise will not persist by taking over your mind.
“Rāhula, develop the meditation that is like water.
For when you develop the meditation that is like water, Rāhula, arisen agreeable and disagreeable contacts will not occupy your mind.
Just as, Rāhula, people wash both clean and unclean things, and even excrement, in water;”
They wash away what has become urine, they wash away what has become saliva, they wash away what has become pus, and they wash away what has become blood;
yet because of this, the water is not distressed, nor ashamed, nor disgusted.
In the same way, Rāhula, develop the meditation that is like water.
“Rāhula, when you develop meditation that is like water, pleasant and unpleasant contacts that arise will not persist by taking over your mind.
Rāhula, develop meditation that is like fire.
For when you develop meditation that is like fire, Rāhula, pleasant and unpleasant contacts that arise will not persist by taking over your mind.”
Just as, Rāhula, fire burns both the pure and the impure— it burns what consists of excrement, what consists of urine,
what consists of saliva, what consists of pus, and what consists of blood—
and yet that fire is not repelled, ashamed, or disgusted by it;
In the same way, Rāhula, develop meditation that is like fire.
For as you develop meditation that is like fire, Rāhula, arisen pleasant and unpleasant contacts will not persist by taking possession of the mind.
Develop meditation that is like wind, Rāhula.
For when you, Rāhula, develop meditation that is like the wind, pleasant and unpleasant contacts that arise will not persist by taking possession of the mind.
Just as, Rāhula, the wind blows upon what is pure and blows upon what is impure;
it blows upon excrement, urine, spittle, pus, and blood.
The wind blows, yet the wind is not distressed, nor does it feel aversion, nor does it feel disgust by that.
In the same way, Rāhula, develop meditation that is like the wind.
For as you develop meditation that is like the wind, Rāhula, pleasant and unpleasant contacts that arise will not persist by taking possession of your mind.
“Rāhula, develop meditation that is like space.

For as you develop meditation that is like space, Rāhula, arisen agreeable and disagreeable contacts will not occupy your mind. Just as space does not rest on anything, so too, Rāhula, developed meditation that is like space—arisen agreeable and disagreeable contacts will not occupy your mind.”
In the same way, Rāhula, cultivate the meditation that is like space.
For as you, Rāhula, cultivate the meditation that is like space, arisen agreeable and disagreeable contacts will not occupy your mind.
Cultivate, Rāhula, the meditation of loving-kindness.
For as you cultivate the meditation on loving-kindness, Rāhula, whatever ill will there may be will be abandoned.
Cultivate the meditation on compassion, Rāhula;
for as you cultivate the meditation on compassion, Rāhula, whatever cruelty there may be will be abandoned.
“Rāhula, develop the meditation on sympathetic joy.
For as you develop the meditation on sympathetic joy, Rāhula, whatever discontent there may be will be abandoned.
Rāhula, develop the meditation on equanimity.”
For as you cultivate the meditation on equanimity, Rāhula, whatever resentment there is will be abandoned.
Cultivate the meditation on foulness, Rāhula;
for as you cultivate the meditation on foulness, Rāhula, whatever lust there is will be abandoned.
“Rāhula, develop the meditation on the perception of impermanence.
For as you develop the meditation on the perception of impermanence, Rāhula, whatever conceit of ‘I am’ there may be will be abandoned.
Develop the meditation on mindfulness of breathing, Rāhula.”
For mindfulness of breathing, Rāhula, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit.
And how, Rāhula, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it is of great fruit and great benefit?

Here, Rāhula, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Thus, being mindful, he breathes in; being mindful, he breathes out.
Breathing in long, he understands: "I am breathing in long"; or breathing out long, he understands:
"I am breathing out long. Breathing in short, he understands: "I am breathing in short"; or breathing out short, he understands: "I am breathing out short."
‘Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself;
‘tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
‘Experiencing rapture, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘experiencing rapture, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure’;
he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing mental formations’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing mental formations’;
he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in tranquilizing the mental formations’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out tranquilizing the mental formations.’
‘Experiencing the mind, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘experiencing the mind, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself;
‘gladdening the mind, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘gladdening the mind, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself;
‘concentrating the mind, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘concentrating the mind, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in liberating the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out liberating the mind.
He trains thus: ‘Contemplating impermanence, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Contemplating impermanence, I shall breathe out.
He trains thus: ‘Contemplating dispassion, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Contemplating dispassion, I shall breathe out.’
‘I shall breathe in contemplating cessation,’ he trains himself; ‘I shall breathe out contemplating cessation,’ he trains himself;
‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment,’ he trains himself; ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment,’ he trains himself.
Thus developed, Rāhula, and thus cultivated, mindfulness of breathing is of great fruit and great benefit.

“Rāhula, when mindfulness of breathing has been developed in this way and cultivated in this way, even those final in-breaths and out-breaths cease having been fully understood, not without being fully understood.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Rāhula was satisfied and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Mahārāhulovādasutta, the second, is finished.
